# API design & refactor

A discipline module — owns endpoint contract discipline, not any one
framework's routing syntax. Combine with whichever stack conventions
skill matches the current repo (`java-conventions`,
`react-conventions`, ... — they ship into a repo as
`.claude/skills/<id>/SKILL.md` and `.cursor/rules/<id>.mdc`).

## Designing a new endpoint

- Resource names are nouns, not verbs — `POST /exports`, not
  `POST /createExport`
- Pagination, filtering, and sorting follow the same convention every
  other endpoint in this API already uses — check an existing endpoint
  before inventing a new pattern
- Error responses share one shape across the whole API (code, message,
  optionally a field-level detail list) — a one-off error format on a
  new endpoint breaks every client's shared error handling
- **When the API already has a documented error convention, name it.**
  This client's contract template names RFC 7807
  `application/problem+json`. A new endpoint adopts the convention that
  exists; it does not invent a second one and leave clients to detect
  which they got at runtime

The full shape of a contract description — conventions, per-endpoint
blocks, shared models, versioning policy — is in
`references/api-contract-template.md`, and
`references/contract-checklist.md` is what to run over a contract before
it goes for review.

## An event is a contract too

This discipline is usually read as REST-shaped, and that leaves the
larger half of a distributed system ungoverned. A domain event that
crosses a service boundary is a published contract with the same
obligations as an endpoint:

- A new or changed event declares its **producer** (exactly one), its
  **known consumers**, its **payload schema**, and its **idempotency
  key** — the field a consumer deduplicates on. Most buses deliver
  at-least-once; with no stated key every consumer invents its own
  answer, and some of them get it wrong
- Changing an event follows the same breaking/non-breaking rules as
  changing an endpoint. Adding an optional field is non-breaking;
  removing or renaming one, changing its type, or changing what it means
  is breaking, and ships as a new event version alongside the old one
- "No consumer uses that field" is only true if the consumer list is —
  which is why the consumer list is part of the contract, and "unknown"
  is an open question rather than a blank

Details and the per-event block: `references/events-template.md`. For a
flow that spans several services, `references/flows-template.md`.

## Field names come from the spec, not from the endpoint

The vocabulary in a payload is the domain's vocabulary. Every field name
uses a term the spec that defined the concept already uses — the same
concept keeps the same name in every endpoint and every event, not
`account_id` in one place and `customerRef` in another.

A term that appears at the API boundary and nowhere in the spec is one
of two things, and both need fixing before the contract ships: it is the
wrong name for a concept that already has one, or it is a real concept
the spec is missing. Coining it at the boundary buries the question
where nobody reviewing the design will see it.

## Backward compatibility

- Never break a published contract without a version bump — adding a
  required field, removing a field, or changing a field's type/meaning
  are all breaking changes, even if "nobody should be relying on that"
- Adding an optional field, a new endpoint, or a new enum value a
  well-behaved client would ignore is non-breaking
- If a change is genuinely breaking, it ships as a new version
  alongside the old one, not as a silent replacement

## Refactoring an existing endpoint

- The contract (request shape, response shape, status codes) is the
  thing being preserved — the implementation underneath is free to
  change completely
- Write or check for a contract test before refactoring internals —
  it's what proves the refactor didn't change behavior a client
  depends on
- If the refactor's goal genuinely requires a contract change, that's
  a new endpoint version, not a "refactor" — call it what it is

## Deprecation

- Deprecating an endpoint means announcing a sunset date and keeping it
  working until then, not returning errors early to force migration
- Point to the replacement explicitly (in docs and, where the protocol
  supports it, in the response itself) — a deprecation notice with no
  stated alternative just creates support tickets
